Every symmetric bilinear form on a finite-dimensional real vector space is congruent to exactly one normal form

$$\operatorname{diag}(I_p,-I_q,0_r),\qquad p+q+r=\dim V.$$

Equivalently, the numbers of positive, negative, and zero diagonal entries are independent of the diagonalizing basis.

$\eta$ has **inertia** $(3,1,0)$: in some (equivalently, in every) basis of
   $V$ in which the matrix of $\eta$ is diagonal, exactly three diagonal
   entries are positive, exactly one is negative, and none is zero
   ([[def-definiteness-inertia-and-signature-data-over-the-reals]]).

derivations.claim: By [L1] the symmetric bilinear form $\eta$ on the finite-dimensional real space $V$ is congruent to exactly one normal form $\operatorname{diag}(I_p,-I_q,0_r)$ with $p+q+r=\dim V=4$, and by [L2] its inertia is $(3,1,0)$; hence $(p,q,r)=(3,1,0)$ and there is a basis $v_0,v_1,v_2,v_3$ of $V$ with $\eta(v_i,v_j)=\operatorname{diag}(1,1,1,-1)_{ij}$ for all $i,j$.

Define the reordering $e_0:=v_3$ and $e_1:=v_0$, $e_2:=v_1$, $e_3:=v_2$. Then $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is an ordered basis of $V$, and evaluating the displayed matrix gives $\eta(e_0,e_0)=-1$, $\eta(e_1,e_1)=\eta(e_2,e_2)=\eta(e_3,e_3)=+1$ and $\eta(e_a,e_b)=0$ for $a\neq b$, that is, $\eta(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$: the required ordered basis exists.

Now let $(f_0,f_1,f_2,f_3)$ be any ordered basis with $\eta(f_a,f_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$. Its matrix is diagonal with diagonal entries $-1,1,1,1$, so in this diagonalizing basis the numbers of positive, negative and zero diagonal entries are $(3,1,0)$; by the uniqueness clause of [L1] the triple $(3,1,0)$ is intrinsic and equals the inertia of $\eta$ given in [L2]. In such a basis exactly one vector, $f_0$, is timelike, because $\eta(f_0,f_0)=-1<0$, and the remaining three are spacelike, because $\eta(f_i,f_i)=+1>0$ for $i=1,2,3$; and this count is exactly the inertia $(3,1,0)$.

boundaries.reason: The hypothesis fixes a 4-dimensional space, so the basis displayed in step 1.1 has four elements and no empty basis or empty index set arises.

boundaries.evidence: Step 1.1: the inertia (3,1,0) has r = 0 zero diagonal entries, and the zero vector is not one of the four basis vectors.
Step 3.1: exactly one basis vector is timelike (the entry -1) and the other three spacelike; the count one-negative/three-positive is verified.
Step 1.1: nondegeneracy with inertia (3,1,0) excludes the degenerate normal forms, so det eta = -1 never vanishes.

boundaries.reason: No interval parameter or boundary index occurs in the existence and counting claims.

boundaries.evidence: Step 1.1 instantiates one basis from Sylvester's existence statement; no simultaneous selection from a family of nonempty sets is made.

boundaries.reason: The Statement asserts existence of a basis plus a universal count in every eta-orthonormal basis, not a biconditional.
No converse direction is claimed; the counting clause is a universal property of eta-orthonormal bases, not the reverse of an equivalence.

There
is an ordered basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $V$ with
$\eta(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$ for all $a,b$.
$\langle v,v\rangle$ is real and nonnegative, and $\langle v,v\rangle=0$ if and only if $v=0$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is).

derivations.claim: By [L1] fix an $\eta$-orthonormal ordered basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $V$. Since it is a basis, $e_0\neq 0$, and by the displayed matrix $\eta(e_0,e_0)=-1<0$.

An inner product must satisfy $\langle v,v\rangle\ge 0$ for every $v$, with equality only at $v=0$, by [L2]. The symmetric bilinear form $\eta$ fails this at the nonzero vector $e_0$, where $\eta(e_0,e_0)=-1<0$; hence $\eta$ is not positive definite and therefore is not an inner product, refuting the displayed statement. The contrast with [L3] shows that the failure comes from $\eta$ itself rather than from the definition of an inner product, which the Euclidean inner product satisfies.

Consequently $\eta$ does not induce a norm on $V$: the Euclidean norm of [L3] is defined as $\lVert x\rVert_2=\sqrt{\langle x,x\rangle}$, and a norm arising from an inner product in this way requires the nonnegative quantity $\langle v,v\rangle$ of [L2] for every $v$, whereas $\eta(e_0,e_0)=-1$ admits no real square root. In particular the positive-definite inner-product theory (Cauchy-Schwarz, norms and orthogonal projection) cannot be applied to $\eta$ without additional argument.

boundaries.reason: The witness is one nonzero vector in a fixed 4-dimensional space; no empty tuple, index set or family occurs.

boundaries.evidence: Step 2.1 uses eta(e_0,e_0) = -1 < 0, while e_0 = 0 is excluded because e_0 is a basis vector of a nonzero space.
Step 1.1: the single vector e_0 already refutes positive definiteness.

boundaries.reason: Nondegeneracy is part of the Lorentz-form hypothesis; no degenerate form or singular parameter case occurs.
No interval or endpoint parameter appears in the refutation.

boundaries.evidence: Step 1.1 selects one element of the nonempty set of eta-orthonormal bases via the existence lemma; a single instantiation, not an arbitrary choice.

boundaries.reason: The refuted claim is not a biconditional; only the positive-definiteness failure is asserted.
There is no converse direction to discharge: the claim is a one-directional property the form fails.

Let $\eta$ be a Lorentz form on a $4$-dimensional real vector space $V$. There
is an ordered basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $V$ with
$\eta(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$ for all $a,b$. Such a basis
is called **$\eta$-orthonormal**; in every $\eta$-orthonormal ordered basis
exactly one basis vector is timelike and the other three are spacelike, and the
count is the inertia $(3,1,0)$ of $\eta$.

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]), let
$n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $v : n \to V$ be a finite list
([[def-linear-combination-and-span]]).

1. **The span of the image of a list.** Whether or not $v$ is injective,
   $$\operatorname{span}(v[n]) \;=\; \Bigl\{\, \sum_{i<n}\lambda_i v_i \;:\; \lambda : n \to F \,\Bigr\} .$$
2. **Coordinates.** $v$ is an ordered basis of $V$ ([[def-linear-basis]]) **if and
   only if** for every $x \in V$ there is **exactly one** $\lambda : n \to F$ with
   $x = \sum_{i<n}\lambda_i v_i$. When that holds, this $\lambda$ is called the
   **coordinate list of $x$ with respect to the ordered basis $v$**, and
   $\lambda_i$ its **$i$-th coordinate**.

The coordinate list is attached to the **ordered** basis and not to the basis as
a set: reordering the list permutes the coordinates of every vector, as the
companion page shows on a worked example in $\mathbb{R}^{2}$.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]), with associated quadratic form
$q(v)=\eta(v,v)$. A vector $v\in V$ is

- **timelike** when $q(v)<0$;
- **null**, or **lightlike**, when $v\neq 0$ and $q(v)=0$;
- **spacelike** when $q(v)>0$;
- **causal** when it is timelike or null.

The zero vector $0\in V$ satisfies $q(0)=0$ and is consequently **none** of
timelike, null or spacelike: the null case explicitly excludes it, and the
timelike and spacelike cases exclude it by $q(0)=0$ together with the strict
inequalities. The **causal character** of a nonzero vector $v$ is the sign of
the real number $q(v)$, and the three names are attached to the three signs as
above. When no confusion arises, the pairing $\eta$ itself is written
$\langle v,w\rangle:=\eta(v,w)$.

**Each nonzero vector has exactly one causal character.** For a nonzero
$v\in V$ the real number $q(v)$ satisfies exactly one of $q(v)<0$, $q(v)=0$,
$q(v)>0$ by trichotomy of the order on $\mathbb R$, so $v$ is timelike, null or
spacelike, and no two of the three alternatives can hold at once. The causal
vectors are therefore exactly the nonzero vectors that are timelike or null,
and the zero vector is causal in no sense introduced here.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

The function induced by an inner product satisfies, for all vectors $u,v$ and scalars $\lambda$,

$$\lVert v\rVert\ge0,\qquad \lVert v\rVert=0\Longleftrightarrow v=0,$$

$$\lVert\lambda v\rVert=|\lambda|\lVert v\rVert,\qquad \lVert u+v\rVert\le\lVert u\rVert+\lVert v\rVert.$$

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]) constructed in this
library ([[def-real-numbers]]) and carrying its order ([[def-real-order]]).

Let $X$ be a set. A **metric** on $X$ is a function
$d : X \times X \to \mathbb{R}$ such that for all $x, y, z \in X$:

- **(M1) Separation.** $d(x,y) = 0$ if and only if $x = y$.
- **(M2) Symmetry.** $d(x,y) = d(y,x)$.
- **(M3) Triangle inequality.** $d(x,z) \le d(x,y) + d(y,z)$.

A **metric space** is a pair $(X,d)$ consisting of a set $X$ and a metric $d$ on
it. The elements of $X$ are its **points** and $d(x,y)$ is the **distance** from
$x$ to $y$. When only one metric is in play we write $X$ for $(X,d)$; when
several are, the metric is always named.

**The values of a metric are real numbers.** The codomain is $\mathbb{R}$, so
$d(x,y)$ is an honest element of the complete ordered field and every
inequality above is an inequality there. No infinite value is permitted;
[[rem-metric-axiom-conventions]] records why extended metrics are not treated in
this library.

**Nonnegativity is deliberately absent from the axiom list.** Many texts add a
fourth axiom $d(x,y) \ge 0$. It is redundant: (M1), (M2) and (M3) already force
it, as [[lem-metric-nonnegativity]] proves. Nothing below assumes it before that
lemma is available.

**Pseudometric.** A **pseudometric** on $X$ is a function
$p : X \times X \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfying (M2), (M3) and the weakening

- **(M1') Reflexivity.** $p(x,x) = 0$ for every $x \in X$

of (M1). A pseudometric may therefore assign distance $0$ to two distinct
points. Every metric is a pseudometric, and a pseudometric is a metric exactly
when $p(x,y) = 0$ forces $x = y$.

**Ultrametric.** An **ultrametric** on $X$ is a metric $d$ that in addition
satisfies

- **(M3') Strong triangle inequality.** $d(x,z) \le \max\{d(x,y), d(y,z)\}$

for all $x, y, z \in X$, where the maximum is that of a two-element subset of
$\mathbb{R}$, which exists and is one of the two elements
([[def-max-min]], [[lem-finite-set-has-max]]). An **ultrametric space** is a pair
$(X,d)$ with $d$ an ultrametric.

A subset $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is **convex** when, for all $x,y\in U$ and $t\in[0,1]$ ([[def-interval]]), the point $(1-t)x+ty$ lies in $U$. Thus the full line segment from $x$ to $y$ remains in $U$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$ and give $\mathbb{R}^n$ the product
topology, which is the metric topology of $d_\infty$
([[lem-product-topology-on-rn]], [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], [[def-metric-topology]]).
Recall that $\mathbb{R}^n$ is a real vector space under coordinatewise operations
([[def-vector-space]], [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]).

A subset $C \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is **convex** when

$$x, y \in C \ \text{ and } \ t \in [0,1] \quad \Longrightarrow \quad (1-t)x + ty \in C$$

([[def-interval]]). Then:

1. **Every convex $C \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is path-connected**
   ([[def-path-connected]]), hence connected ([[def-connected-space]],
   [[thm-path-connected-implies-connected]]).
2. **Every ball is convex**, in each of the norms $\lVert\cdot\rVert_1$,
   $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$, $\lVert\cdot\rVert_\infty$
   ([[def-p-norms-on-rn]], [[def-metric-ball]]); so every ball of
   $\mathbb{R}^n$ is path-connected and connected.
3. **$\mathbb{R}^n$ itself is convex**, hence path-connected and connected, and
   so is every half-space
   $\{\, x : x_k \le c \,\}$, and every box $\prod_{k<n} J_k$ with each $J_k$ an
   order-convex subset of $\mathbb{R}$.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]).

A subset $U \subseteq X$ is **open in $(X,d)$** if for every $x \in U$ there is a
real $r > 0$ with $B(x,r) \subseteq U$ ([[def-metric-ball]]). A subset
$F \subseteq X$ is **closed in $(X,d)$** if its complement $X \setminus F$ is
open.

The collection

$$\mathcal{T}_d := \{\, U \subseteq X : U \text{ is open in } (X,d) \,\}$$

of all open subsets is the **metric topology** of $d$ on $X$. A subset of $X$
that is both open and closed is called **clopen**.

**Two sets are open for trivial reasons.** $\emptyset$ is open, because the
defining condition quantifies over no points; and $X$ is open, because
$B(x,r) \subseteq X$ for every $x$ and every $r > 0$. Consequently $X$ and
$\emptyset$ are also closed, and both are clopen.

**A neighbourhood of a point $x$** is any set containing an open set that
contains $x$; an **open neighbourhood** is an open set containing $x$. In a
metric space, a set is a neighbourhood of $x$ exactly when it contains some
ball $B(x,r)$ with $r>0$. Thus $U$ is open exactly when it is a neighbourhood of
each of its points, and metric balls suffice to test this condition.

**The metric, not the set, determines $\mathcal{T}_d$.** Two metrics on the same
set may have different metric topologies, and two different metrics may have the
same one; the systematic comparison is [[def-equivalent-metrics]].

Let $(X, \mathcal{T})$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]).

- A **separation** of $X$ is an ordered pair $(U, V)$ of **open**, **nonempty**,
  **disjoint** subsets of $X$ with $U \cup V = X$.
- $X$ is **disconnected** when a separation of $X$ exists, and **connected** when
  none does.
- A subset $A \subseteq X$ is a **connected subset** of $X$ when the space
  $(A, \mathcal{T}_A)$ is connected, $\mathcal{T}_A$ being the subspace topology
  ([[def-subspace-topology-top]]). "Disconnected subset" is read the same way.

Since $U$ and $V$ are complementary in $X$, each of them is closed as well as
open; so a separation is the same thing as a partition of $X$ into two nonempty
clopen pieces ([[def-topological-space]]). The **clopen** subsets of $X$ are
those that are both open and closed, and $\varnothing$ and $X$ are always among
them.

**The empty space and the one-point space are connected in this library.**
Neither admits a separation: a separation requires two nonempty disjoint sets
whose union is the whole space, and neither $\varnothing$ nor a singleton can be
written as such a union. So both are connected under the definition above,
without any special clause. **This is a live convention fork** and the competing
choice is recorded in [[rem-connectedness-conventions]]; nothing on this page
depends on which is taken except the reading of the word "connected" applied to
those two spaces.

**Connectedness is a property of a space, not of an ambient pair.** The condition
above mentions only $(X,\mathcal{T})$. When it is applied to $A \subseteq X$ it
is applied to the space $(A, \mathcal{T}_A)$, so it does not change if $A$ is
regarded as a subspace of some other space inducing the same topology on $A$; in
particular a subset of $A$ is connected as a subset of $A$ exactly when it is
connected as a subset of $X$, by transitivity of the subspace topology
([[def-subspace-topology-top]]). This is why "connected" may be used of a subset
with no ambient space named.

**Spelled out for a subset.** $A \subseteq X$ is disconnected exactly when there
are open $U, V \subseteq X$ with

$$A \subseteq U \cup V, \qquad U \cap A \ne \varnothing, \qquad V \cap A \ne \varnothing, \qquad U \cap V \cap A = \varnothing,$$

because the open sets of $(A,\mathcal{T}_A)$ are precisely the traces $U \cap A$.
Note the last condition: it asks $U$ and $V$ to be disjoint **on $A$**, not in
$X$. Requiring $U \cap V = \varnothing$ outright is a strictly stronger demand
and is a different notion.

**The two-point discrete space.** Write $\mathbf{2} := \{0,1\}$ with the discrete
topology ([[def-standard-topologies]]), in which every subset is open. A
separation of $X$ is the same datum as a surjective continuous map
$X \to \mathbf{2}$ ([[def-continuous-map-top]]): given $(U,V)$, the map sending
$U$ to $0$ and $V$ to $1$ is continuous because the preimage of each of the four
open subsets of $\mathbf{2}$ is one of $\varnothing$, $U$, $V$, $X$; given a
surjective continuous $\chi : X \to \mathbf{2}$, the pair
$(\chi^{-1}[\{0\}], \chi^{-1}[\{1\}])$ is a separation. This reformulation is
proved as a theorem on this page and is recorded here only to name $\mathbf{2}$.

**Separated sets.** Two subsets $A_1, A_2 \subseteq X$ are **separated in $X$**
when

$$\overline{A_1} \cap A_2 = \varnothing \qquad \text{and} \qquad A_1 \cap \overline{A_2} = \varnothing,$$

closures taken in $X$ ([[def-interior-closure-boundary-top]],
[[thm-closure-characterisation-top]]). Separated sets are disjoint, since
$A_1 \subseteq \overline{A_1}$; the converse fails. This is verbatim the
condition [[def-connected-r]] uses on the real line, transported to an arbitrary
space, and the theorem relating it to the definition above is the next lemma on
this page.

**Totally disconnected spaces, and the empty case.** The vocabulary for a space
all of whose connected subsets are single points is fixed later on this page,
together with the components; it is not defined here because it is stated in
terms of components.

Let $(X, \mathcal{T})$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]) and let
$S \subseteq X$. The **subspace topology** (also *relative topology*) on $S$ is

$$\mathcal{T}_S := \{\, U \cap S : U \in \mathcal{T} \,\},$$

the family of **traces** on $S$ of the open sets of $X$. The pair
$(S, \mathcal{T}_S)$ is a **subspace** of $X$. A subset of $S$ that lies in
$\mathcal{T}_S$ is said to be **open in $S$**, and *relatively open* where the
ambient space needs emphasis.

**$\mathcal{T}_S$ is a topology, and this is discharged here.** (T1):
$\varnothing = \varnothing \cap S$ and $S = X \cap S$ are traces. (T2): if
$\mathcal{S}' \subseteq \mathcal{T}_S$, choose for each member a set of
$\mathcal{T}$ tracing to it — no choice principle is needed, since
$U' := \bigcup \{\, U \in \mathcal{T} : U \cap S \subseteq W \,\}$ is a canonical
such set for $W \in \mathcal{T}_S$, being open by (T2) in $X$ and satisfying
$U' \cap S = W$ — and then
$\bigcup_i (U_i \cap S) = (\bigcup_i U_i) \cap S \in \mathcal{T}_S$ by (T2) in
$X$. (T3): $(U \cap S) \cap (V \cap S) = (U \cap V) \cap S \in \mathcal{T}_S$ by
(T3) in $X$.

**Closed sets of a subspace are the traces of the closed sets.** A set
$C \subseteq S$ is closed in $S$ if and only if $C = F \cap S$ for some closed
$F \subseteq X$. Indeed $S \setminus (U \cap S) = (X \setminus U) \cap S$ and
$S \setminus (F \cap S) = (X \setminus F) \cap S$, so complementation inside $S$
matches complementation inside $X$ under tracing.

**Bases and subbases trace as well.** If $\mathcal{B}$ is a basis for
$\mathcal{T}$ ([[def-topology-basis-subbasis]]) then
$\mathcal{B}_S := \{\, B \cap S : B \in \mathcal{B} \,\}$ is a basis for
$\mathcal{T}_S$: its members are open in $S$, and for $W = U \cap S$ open in $S$
and $x \in W$ there is $B \in \mathcal{B}$ with $x \in B \subseteq U$, whence
$x \in B \cap S \subseteq W$. The same computation with a subbasis $\mathcal{S}$
shows that $\{\, S_0 \cap S : S_0 \in \mathcal{S} \,\}$ is a subbasis for
$\mathcal{T}_S$, since tracing commutes with finite intersections and with
unions.

**The inclusion is continuous.** The inclusion map $\iota : S \to X$,
$\iota(s) = s$, satisfies $\iota^{-1}[U] = U \cap S$ for every $U \subseteq X$,
so preimages of open sets are open and $\iota$ is continuous
([[thm-continuity-characterisations-top]], clause (b)). Moreover
$\mathcal{T}_S$ is the **coarsest** topology on $S$ making $\iota$ continuous: any
topology on $S$ for which $\iota$ is continuous must contain every
$\iota^{-1}[U] = U \cap S$, hence contain $\mathcal{T}_S$.

**Characteristic property of a map into a subspace.** Let $(Z, \mathcal{T}_Z)$ be
a topological space and let $g : Z \to S$ be a function. Then

$$g \text{ is continuous as a map } Z \to (S,\mathcal{T}_S) \iff \iota \circ g \text{ is continuous as a map } Z \to (X,\mathcal{T}) .$$

*Proof.* For $U \in \mathcal{T}$ one has
$(\iota \circ g)^{-1}[U] = g^{-1}[\iota^{-1}[U]] = g^{-1}[U \cap S]$. If $g$ is
continuous then each $g^{-1}[U \cap S]$ is open, so $\iota \circ g$ is continuous;
conversely if $\iota \circ g$ is continuous then for any $W = U \cap S$ open in
$S$ the set $g^{-1}[W] = (\iota \circ g)^{-1}[U]$ is open, so $g$ is continuous.
Both directions use only clause (b) of [[thm-continuity-characterisations-top]].

**Restriction of a continuous map.** If $f : X \to Y$ is continuous and
$S \subseteq X$, then $f|_S : S \to Y$ is continuous, since
$(f|_S)^{-1}[V] = f^{-1}[V] \cap S$ is open in $S$ for every open $V \subseteq Y$
([[def-continuous-map-top]], [[thm-continuity-characterisations-top]]).

**When relative and ambient agree.** If $S$ is open in $X$ then a subset of $S$
is open in $S$ if and only if it is open in $X$: a trace $U \cap S$ is then an
intersection of two open sets of $X$, and conversely an open subset of $X$
contained in $S$ is its own trace. The same statement with "closed" throughout
holds when $S$ is closed in $X$. Both are used in the pasting lemma of the next
item, and both fail without the hypothesis: $S$ itself is always open and closed
in $S$, and need be neither in $X$.

Let $(X, \mathcal{T})$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]), with
subsets carrying the subspace topology ([[def-subspace-topology-top]]) and
connectedness as in [[def-connected-space]]. Let $x \in X$.

- The **connected component of $x$** is
  $$C(x) \;:=\; \bigcup \{\, A \subseteq X : x \in A \text{ and } A \text{ is connected} \,\} .$$
  A **component of $X$** is a set of the form $C(x)$ for some $x \in X$.
- The **quasicomponent of $x$** is
  $$Q(x) \;:=\; \bigcap \{\, K \subseteq X : x \in K \text{ and } K \text{ is clopen in } X \,\} .$$
  A **quasicomponent of $X$** is a set of the form $Q(x)$.
- $X$ is **totally disconnected** when $C(x) = \{x\}$ for every $x \in X$.

**Both are well posed, and the obligations are discharged here.** The family
united in the definition of $C(x)$ is nonempty, since the singleton $\{x\}$ is
connected: a singleton admits no separation, a separation requiring two disjoint
nonempty pieces. Every member of that family contains $x$, so
[[thm-unions-of-connected-sets]] claim 1 applies and **$C(x)$ is connected**;
being a union of every connected set through $x$, it contains each of them, so
$C(x)$ is *the largest connected subset of $X$ containing $x$*. The family
intersected in the definition of $Q(x)$ is nonempty as well, since $X$ itself is
clopen ([[def-topological-space]]), so the intersection is a set; it contains
$x$, every member doing so.

**Both notions are defined by a property of $X$, not of an ambient space.** A
component of a subspace $S \subseteq X$ means a component of the space $S$, and
is written $C_S(y)$ when the space needs naming. The same holds for
quasicomponents.

**Totally disconnected, spelled out.** $X$ is totally disconnected exactly when
every connected subset of $X$ has at most one point: if some connected $A$ had
two points $x \ne y$ then $A \subseteq C(x)$ would give $C(x) \ne \{x\}$, and
conversely if $C(x) \ne \{x\}$ then $C(x)$ is a connected set with at least two
points. The empty space is totally disconnected, having no point to test.

**A discrete space is totally disconnected.** Let $X$ carry the discrete topology
([[def-standard-topologies]]) and let $A \subseteq X$ have two distinct points
$x, y$. Every subset of $A$ is open in $A$, so $(\{x\}, A \setminus \{x\})$ is a
pair of open, disjoint, nonempty sets covering $A$, that is a separation. Hence
no connected subset has two points and every component is a singleton. The
converse fails: total disconnectedness does not force the topology to be
discrete.

Let $X$ be a topological space, with subsets carrying the subspace topology
([[def-subspace-topology-top]]). Then:

1. **The unit interval is connected.** $I = [0,1]$ is a connected subset of
   $\mathbb{R}$, hence a connected space.
2. **Path-connected implies connected.** If $X$ is path-connected
   ([[def-path-connected]]) then $X$ is connected ([[def-connected-space]]). The
   same holds for a subset: a path-connected subset of $X$ is a connected subset
   of $X$.
3. **Path components refine components.** For every $x \in X$,
   $$P(x) \;\subseteq\; C(x),$$
   the path component inside the component
   ([[def-connected-component-and-quasicomponent]]). So every component is a
   union of path components.

**No converse is claimed.** Claim 2 is one-directional and claim 3 is an
inclusion; the question of when a connected space is path-connected is not
settled here.

**No choice principle is used.** The proof takes the union over the **set of all**
paths issuing from a fixed point rather than selecting one path per endpoint,
which is what an appeal to the Axiom of Choice would be. The point at which the
temptation arises is flagged in the remarks.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \le b$, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on the closed bounded interval $[a,b]$ ([[def-interval]],
[[def-continuity-real]]), and let $y \in \mathbb{R}$ satisfy

$$f(a) \le y \le f(b) \qquad \text{or} \qquad f(b) \le y \le f(a) .$$

Then there is $c \in [a,b]$ with $f(c) = y$.

**The construction is canonical, so no choice principle is used.** The bisection
below tests the left half first and takes the right half only when the left one
has been ruled out, so the passage from one interval to the next is a *function*
of that interval, and [[thm-recursion]] applies with nothing selected. This is
the same discipline the library uses wherever a sequence is built one term at a
time.

**Completeness of $\mathbb{R}$ is what does the work.** The bisection produces a
nested sequence of closed bounded intervals whose lengths tend to $0$, and it is
[[thm-nested-interval-property]] — hence the least-upper-bound property — that
supplies the point. Over an ordered field that is not complete the theorem
fails; the witness for that, stated for an arbitrary ordered field and worked
over $\mathbb{Q}$, is
[[cex-evt-and-ivt-fail-over-a-non-complete-field]], which states its own
$\varepsilon$-$\delta$ continuity inline and is not an instance of this page's
definition.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]), with causal terminology as in
[[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]], and let

$$T:=\{v\in V:\eta(v,v)<0\}$$

be its **timelike set**. By [[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]] the
set $T$ has exactly two connected components, and each of them is nonempty,
open, convex and path-connected. A **time orientation** of $(V,\eta)$ is a
choice of one of these two components. Fixing such a choice, write $C^+$ for the
chosen component and

$$C^-:=T\setminus C^+$$

for the other component; thus $T=C^+\sqcup C^-$ is a disjoint union and
$C^+$, $C^-$ are exactly the two components supplied by the lemma. Relative to
this choice a vector $v\in V$ is

- **future timelike** when $v\in C^+$;
- **past timelike** when $v\in C^-$;
- **future null** when $v\neq 0$, $\eta(v,v)=0$ and $v\in\operatorname{cl}(C^+)$;
- **past null** when $v\neq 0$, $\eta(v,v)=0$ and $v\in\operatorname{cl}(C^-)$;
- **future causal** when it is future timelike or future null;
- **past causal** when it is past timelike or past null.

The sets $\operatorname{cl}(C^+)$ and $\operatorname{cl}(C^-)$ are the
**future closed cone** and the **past closed cone** of the time-oriented space
$(V,\eta,C^+)$. By [[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]] each of them
is a convex cone, their intersection is $\{0\}$, and a vector is causal exactly
when it is future causal or past causal, in which case exactly one of these two
alternatives holds: no nonzero vector is both future causal and past causal.
The timelike vectors are exactly the points of $T=C^+\cup C^-$, and
$0\notin T$ because $\eta(0,0)=0$; since a null vector is nonzero with
$\eta(v,v)=0$, no vector is both timelike and null, so the classes above are
mutually exclusive where the definitions say they are: no vector is both future
and past causal, and no timelike vector is null.

derivations.claim: For $v=\sum_av^ae_a$ and $w=\sum_bw^be_b$, bilinearity of $\eta$ together with $\eta(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$ from [L1] give $\eta(v,w)=-v^0w^0+v^1w^1+v^2w^2+v^3w^3$, hence $\eta(v,v)=-(v^0)^2+\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert^2$, where $\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert^2=(v^1)^2+(v^2)^2+(v^3)^2=\lVert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rVert_2^2$ by [L4]. The assignment $c(v):=(v^0,v^1,v^2,v^3)$ is a bijection $V\to\mathbb R^4$ by [L2]. By [L3] the timelike set is $T=\{v:\eta(v,v)<0\}=\{v:(v^0)^2>\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert^2\}=\{v:\lvert v^0\rvert>\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\}=T_+\cup T_-$, because $\lvert v^0\rvert>\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert$ holds exactly when $v^0>\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert$ or $v^0<-\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert$.

Define $d(u,w):=\lVert c(u)-c(w)\rVert_2$. By [L5] applied to the Euclidean inner product of [L4], the Euclidean norm is nonnegative, vanishes only at $0$, is absolutely homogeneous, and satisfies the triangle inequality; with $c$ a bijection [L2] this shows that $d$ is a metric on $V$ in the sense of [L6]: $d(u,w)=0$ if and only if $c(u)=c(w)$, if and only if $u=w$; $d(u,w)=d(w,u)$ by $\lVert-x\rVert=\lVert x\rVert$; and $d(u,w)\le d(u,z)+d(z,w)$ by the triangle inequality applied to $(c(u)-c(z))+(c(z)-c(w))$.

The coordinate image $c(T_+)=\{x\in\mathbb R^4:x_0>\lVert x_{\mathrm{vec}}\rVert_2\}$ is convex in the sense of [L7]: if $x,y\in c(T_+)$ and $t\in[0,1]$, then the first coordinate of $z:=(1-t)x+ty$ is $z_0=(1-t)x_0+ty_0>(1-t)\lVert x_{\mathrm{vec}}\rVert_2+t\lVert y_{\mathrm{vec}}\rVert_2\ge\lVert(1-t)x_{\mathrm{vec}}+ty_{\mathrm{vec}}\rVert_2=\lVert z_{\mathrm{vec}}\rVert_2$, where the strict inequality uses $x_0>\lVert x_{\mathrm{vec}}\rVert_2$, $y_0>\lVert y_{\mathrm{vec}}\rVert_2$ and $t,1-t\ge0$ and the second inequality is the triangle inequality with homogeneity from [L5]; hence $z\in c(T_+)$. The same computation with reversed inequalities shows that $c(T_-)=\{x:x_0<-\lVert x_{\mathrm{vec}}\rVert_2\}$ is convex.

The coordinate vector of $e_0$ is $(1,0,0,0)$ and that of $-e_0$ is $(-1,0,0,0)$, by uniqueness of coordinates [L2]; hence $e_0\in T_+$ and $-e_0\in T_-$, so both sets are nonempty. If $v\in T_+\cap T_-$, then $v^0>\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\ge0$ and $v^0<-\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\le0$ simultaneously, which is impossible; hence $T_+$ and $T_-$ are disjoint and $T=T_+\sqcup T_-$.

Let $f(v):=v^0-\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert$. For all $u,w\in V$ one has $\lvert u^0-w^0\rvert\le d(u,w)$, because $(u^0-w^0)^2$ is one term of the sum $\lVert c(u)-c(w)\rVert_2^2$, and $\bigl\lvert\lvert u_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert-\lvert w_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\bigr\rvert\le\lVert u_{\mathrm{vec}}-w_{\mathrm{vec}}\rVert_2\le d(u,w)$, the first inequality from $\lvert u_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\le\lVert u_{\mathrm{vec}}-w_{\mathrm{vec}}\rVert_2+\lvert w_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert$ and its symmetric partner by [L5] and the second because the last three coordinate squares form a sub-sum; hence $\lvert f(u)-f(w)\rvert\le2d(u,w)$. If $f(v)>0$ and $d(u,v)<f(v)/2$, then $f(u)\ge f(v)-2d(u,v)>0$; therefore $T_+=\{v:f(v)>0\}$ is open in the metric topology of [L9], since the ball of radius $f(v)/2$ about each of its points lies in it, and the same argument with $g(v):=-v^0-\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert$ shows that $T_-=\{v:g(v)>0\}$ is open.

By step 2.1 the sets $c(T_+)$ and $c(T_-)$ are convex subsets of $\mathbb R^4$, hence path-connected by [L8]. Let $p:[0,1]\to c(T_+)$ be a path in $c(T_+)$ and put $\gamma(t):=c^{-1}(p(t))$, a map into $T_+$ because $c$ is a bijection; then $d(\gamma(s),\gamma(t))=\lVert p(s)-p(t)\rVert_2$ for all $s,t$, so for every $\eta>0$ the $\delta>0$ supplied by continuity of $p$ at $t$ gives $d(\gamma(s),\gamma(t))<\eta$ whenever $\lvert s-t\rvert<\delta$: thus $\gamma$ is a path in the metric space $(V,d)$, and $T_+$ is path-connected. The same argument gives that $T_-$ is path-connected. By [L13] the path-connected sets $T_+$ and $T_-$ are connected subsets of $T$, and by step 2.2 they are nonempty with $T=T_+\sqcup T_-$.

Suppose $C\subseteq T$ is a connected subset meeting both $T_+$ and $T_-$. The sets $C\cap T_+$ and $C\cap T_-$ are open in the subspace topology on $C$ by step 2.3 and [L11], they are nonempty because $C$ meets both, they are disjoint, and their union is $C$ because $C\subseteq T=T_+\sqcup T_-$ by step 1.1; thus $(C\cap T_+,C\cap T_-)$ is a separation of $C$ in the sense of [L10], contradicting connectedness of $C$. Hence every connected subset of $T$ is contained in $T_+$ or in $T_-$.

The identity $\operatorname{cl}(T_+)=\{v:f(v)\ge0\}$ holds for the closure in the metric topology of [L9]: if $f(v)<0$, then every $u$ with $d(u,v)<-f(v)/2$ has $f(u)<0$ by the Lipschitz bound of step 2.3, so a ball about $v$ misses $T_+=\{f>0\}$ and $v\notin\operatorname{cl}(T_+)$; conversely, if $f(v)\ge0$, then for every real $t>0$ the point $v+te_0$ has coordinates $(v^0+t,v^1,v^2,v^3)$ by [L2], hence $f(v+te_0)=f(v)+t>0$, so $v+te_0\in T_+$ and $d(v+te_0,v)=t\to0$. The same argument with $g(v)=-v^0-\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert$ gives $\operatorname{cl}(T_-)=\{v:g(v)\ge0\}$; in coordinates these are the displayed sets $\{v:v^0\ge\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\}$ and $\{v:v^0\le-\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\}$.

Let $\gamma:[0,1]\to T$ be a path with $\gamma(0)\in T_+$ and $\gamma(1)\in T_-$, and put $h(t):=(\gamma(t))^0$. Using the bound $\lvert u^0-w^0\rvert\le d(u,w)$ of step 2.3, for every $\eta>0$ the $\delta>0$ supplied by continuity of $\gamma$ at $t$ gives $\lvert h(s)-h(t)\rvert\le d(\gamma(s),\gamma(t))<\eta$ whenever $\lvert s-t\rvert<\delta$; hence $h$ is continuous on $[0,1]$ in the sense required by [L14], with $h(0)>0$ because $\gamma(0)\in T_+$ and $h(1)<0$ because $\gamma(1)\in T_-$. By [L14] there is $t\in[0,1]$ with $h(t)=0$; but $\gamma(t)\in T$ gives $(h(t))^2=(\gamma(t)^0)^2>\lvert\gamma(t)_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert^2\ge0$ by step 1.1, so $h(t)\neq0$, a contradiction. Hence no path in $T$ joins $T_+$ to $T_-$.

By step 3.1 the sets $T_+$ and $T_-$ are connected, and by step 2.2 they are nonempty and disjoint with $T=T_+\sqcup T_-$. Let $x\in T_+$. By [L12] the component $C_T(x)$ is the largest connected subset of $T$ containing $x$; since $T_+$ is a connected subset of $T$ containing $x$, one has $T_+\subseteq C_T(x)$, while $C_T(x)$ is connected and contains $x\in T_+$, so step 3.2 gives $C_T(x)\subseteq T_+$; hence $C_T(x)=T_+$. The same argument with $x\in T_-$ gives $C_T(x)=T_-$. Therefore $T_+$ and $T_-$ are exactly the connected components of $T$, and since $T=T_+\sqcup T_-$ these are all of them.

If $v\in\operatorname{cl}(T_+)\cap\operatorname{cl}(T_-)$, then step 3.3 gives $v^0\ge\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert$ and $v^0\le-\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert$, hence $0\le2\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\le0$, so $\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert=0$ and $v^0=0$; all coordinates of $v$ vanish, and uniqueness of coordinates [L2] gives $v=0$. Conversely $0$ lies in both displayed sets of step 3.3, hence in both closures. Therefore $\operatorname{cl}(T_+)\cap\operatorname{cl}(T_-)=\{0\}$.

The descriptions of step 3.3 also show that $\operatorname{cl}(T_+)$ and $\operatorname{cl}(T_-)$ are convex cones and that the nonzero causal vectors are exactly the nonzero points of their union. For the cone property, if $v,w\in\operatorname{cl}(T_+)$ and $\lambda\ge0$, then $(v+w)^0=v^0+w^0\ge\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert+\lvert w_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\ge\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}+w_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert$ and $(\lambda v)^0=\lambda v^0\ge\lambda\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert=\lvert\lambda v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert$ by [L5], so $v+w,\lambda v\in\operatorname{cl}(T_+)$, and reversing the inequalities gives the same for $\operatorname{cl}(T_-)$. For the classification, every timelike vector lies in $T=T_+\cup T_-\subseteq\operatorname{cl}(T_+)\cup\operatorname{cl}(T_-)$ by step 1.1, and every null vector $v$ has $\lvert v^0\rvert=\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert$ by step 1.1, hence lies in $\operatorname{cl}(T_+)\cup\operatorname{cl}(T_-)$ by step 3.3; conversely a nonzero $v$ in that union satisfies $\lvert v^0\rvert\ge\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert$, hence $\eta(v,v)=-(v^0)^2+\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert^2\le0$ by step 1.1, and is therefore timelike or null, that is, causal, by [L3].

Let $(e'_0,e'_1,e'_2,e'_3)$ be another $\eta$-orthonormal ordered basis with coordinate map $c'$ and distance $d'(u,w):=\lVert c'(u)-c'(w)\rVert_2$; then $c'=Mc$ for the change-of-basis matrix $M$ between the two ordered bases, which is invertible because both are bases [L2]. For any real matrix $N$ put $K(N):=\bigl(\sum_a(\sum_b\lvert N_{ab}\rvert)^2\bigr)^{1/2}$; each component of $Nx$ satisfies $\lvert(Nx)_a\rvert\le(\max_b\lvert x_b\rvert)\sum_b\lvert N_{ab}\rvert\le\lVert x\rVert_2\sum_b\lvert N_{ab}\rvert$ by [L5], so $\lVert Nx\rVert_2\le K(N)\lVert x\rVert_2$, and applying this to $M$ and to $M^{-1}$ with $\kappa:=\max\bigl(K(M),K(M^{-1}),1\bigr)\ge1$ gives $\kappa^{-1}\lVert x\rVert_2\le\lVert Mx\rVert_2\le\kappa\lVert x\rVert_2$ for every $x$; hence $d'$ and $d$ determine the same open sets, the same closures and the same connected subsets, so the components of $T$ and the openness and closure claims of this lemma are intrinsic, independent of which $\eta$-orthonormal basis defines the coordinates. Since the argument of steps 1.1 through 4.3 used only that $(e'_0,e'_1,e'_2,e'_3)$ is $\eta$-orthonormal, it applies verbatim in the primed coordinates and shows that the primed coordinate sets $\{v:v'^0>\lvert v'_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\}$ and $\{v:v'^0<-\lvert v'_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\}$ are also exactly the two components of $T$; hence the primed pair coincides with the unordered pair $\{T_+,T_-\}$. By [L15] a time orientation is a choice of one of these two components, so the two displayed coordinate sets coincide with the chosen $C^+$ and its complement $C^-$ in some order, possibly the reverse of a previously fixed naming; in particular the description is basis-independent up to that interchange.

citations.quote:
There
is an ordered basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $V$ with
$\eta(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$ for all $a,b$.
An **orientation** of $V$ is an equivalence class of ordered bases under this relation; a basis in the chosen class is **positively oriented** for that orientation.

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space
([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]), with orientation fixed as a positive ray of
the determinant line $\Lambda^4V$
([[def-determinant-line-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]])
and with the corresponding class of positively oriented ordered bases of $V$
([[def-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]]); by
[[prop-orientations-and-positive-basis-classes-agree-in-positive-dimension]] the
positive ray selects exactly one such class for $\dim V=4>0$.

An **inertial frame** of the model is a tuple $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ consisting
of an event $o\in A$ and an ordered basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $V$ that is

1. **$\eta$-orthonormal**: $\eta(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$ for all $a,b$ ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]]);
2. **future**: $e_0\in C^+$, i.e. $e_0$ is future timelike; and
3. **positively oriented**: the ordered basis lies in the positive-basis class
   selected by the fixed orientation.

The event $o$ is the **origin** of the frame and $e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$ are its
**basis vectors**.

**Inertial charts.** For an inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$, define

$$E:\mathbb R^4\longrightarrow V,\qquad E(u):=\sum_{a=0}^3u^ae_a .$$

Then $E$ is a linear isomorphism ([[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]]):
it is linear by construction, and it is bijective because
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is an ordered basis, every $v\in V$ having exactly one
coordinate list $u$ with $v=\sum_au^ae_a$
([[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]). The **inertial
chart** of the frame is the map

$$x:A\longrightarrow\mathbb R^4,\qquad x(p):=E^{-1}(p-o),$$

and its values $x^a(p)$ are the **inertial coordinates of the event $p$** in the
frame. Since $E$ and $v\mapsto p+v$ are bijections, $x$ is a bijection
$A\to\mathbb R^4$; and $x(p)=0$ exactly when $p-o=0_V$, that is, exactly when
$p=o$.

**Transition law.** Let $(o';e'_0,e'_1,e'_2,e'_3)$ be another inertial frame
with chart $x'$, and let $M=(M^b_a)$ be the change-of-basis matrix defined by
$e'_a=\sum_bM^b_ae_b$, a $4\times4$ real matrix that is invertible because both
families are ordered bases. Then $E'(u)=\sum_au^ae'_a=E(Mu)$ for all
$u\in\mathbb R^4$, for the matrix-vector product $Mu$ in the coordinates of the
first frame, because $\sum_au^a\sum_bM^b_ae_b=\sum_b(\sum_aM^b_au^a)e_b$; hence
$E'=E\circ M$ and $E'^{-1}=M^{-1}\circ E^{-1}$, so for every event $p$,

$$x'(p)=M^{-1}\bigl(x(p)-x(o')\bigr)=M^{-1}x(p)-M^{-1}x(o') .$$

In particular the transition between two inertial charts is an affine map of
$\mathbb R^4$ with invertible linear part $M^{-1}$ and constant part
$-M^{-1}x(o')$, and it is a bijection of $\mathbb R^4$ with inverse
$u\mapsto Mu+x(o')$, which is the transition in the reverse direction.

**The inertial atlas.** The **inertial atlas** of the model is the family of
all inertial frames together with their inertial charts. Its charts are
available at every event by [[lem-future-oriented-inertial-frames-exist]], which
supplies for every $o\in A$ an inertial frame with origin $o$; and any two of
its charts are related by the affine transition displayed above.
If $\det T>0$, then $T$ carries every positively oriented basis to a positively oriented basis; if $\det T<0$, then $T$ carries every positively oriented basis to a negatively oriented one.

A **Lorentz form** on $V$ is a symmetric bilinear form
$\eta:V\times V\to\mathbb R$ ([[def-bilinear-symmetric-skew-and-alternating-forms]])
such that

1.

Write
$v=v^0e_0+v^1e_1+v^2e_2+v^3e_3$ for the coordinates of $v$
([[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]) and

$$\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert:=\sqrt{(v^1)^2+(v^2)^2+(v^3)^2}.$$

is independent of the diagonalizing basis by Sylvester's law of inertia
([[def-definiteness-inertia-and-signature-data-over-the-reals]]); hence clause 2

negative entry followed by three positive entries. No positive-definite

([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]). Two vectors $u,v\in V$ are
**$\eta$-orthogonal**, written $u\perp v$, when $\eta(u,v)=0$. For a subset
$S\subseteq V$ the **orthogonal complement** of $S$ is

$$S^{\perp}:=\{v\in V:\eta(v,s)=0\text{ for every }s\in S\},$$

and for a vector $u$ one writes $u^{\perp}:=\{u\}^{\perp}$.

- $S^{\perp}$ is a linear subspace of $V$: if $v,w\in S^{\perp}$ and
  $\lambda\in\mathbb R$, then for every $s\in S$ bilinearity gives
  $\eta(v+\lambda w,s)=\eta(v,s)+\lambda\eta(w,s)=0$, so $v+\lambda w\in S^{\perp}$.
  In particular the zero vector lies in $S^{\perp}$ and $S^{\perp}$ is never
  empty.

  $v\in S^{\perp}$ by the definition of $S^{\perp}$, and symmetry of $\eta$
  gives $\eta(s,v)=0$ for every $v\in S^{\perp}$, that is,
  $s\in(S^{\perp})^{\perp}$.
- $S^{\perp}=(\operatorname{span}S)^{\perp}$: the inclusion
  $S\subseteq\operatorname{span}S$ gives
  $(\operatorname{span}S)^{\perp}\subseteq S^{\perp}$; conversely, if

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]). Two vectors $u,v\in V$ are
**$\eta$-orthogonal**, written $u\perp v$, when $\eta(u,v)=0$. For a subset
$S\subseteq V$ the **orthogonal complement** of $S$ is

$$S^{\perp}:=\{v\in V:\eta(v,s)=0\text{ for every }s\in S\},$$

and for a vector $u$ one writes $u^{\perp}:=\{u\}^{\perp}$.

**Elementary properties.** For every subset $S\subseteq V$:

- $S^{\perp}$ is a linear subspace of $V$: if $v,w\in S^{\perp}$ and
  $\lambda\in\mathbb R$, then for every $s\in S$ bilinearity gives
  $\eta(v+\lambda w,s)=\eta(v,s)+\lambda\eta(w,s)=0$, so $v+\lambda w\in S^{\perp}$.
  In particular the zero vector lies in $S^{\perp}$ and $S^{\perp}$ is never
  empty.
- $S\subseteq (S^{\perp})^{\perp}$: if $s\in S$, then $\eta(v,s)=0$ for every
  $v\in S^{\perp}$ by the definition of $S^{\perp}$, and symmetry of $\eta$
  gives $\eta(s,v)=0$ for every $v\in S^{\perp}$, that is,
  $s\in(S^{\perp})^{\perp}$.
- $S^{\perp}=(\operatorname{span}S)^{\perp}$: the inclusion
  $S\subseteq\operatorname{span}S$ gives
  $(\operatorname{span}S)^{\perp}\subseteq S^{\perp}$; conversely, if
  $v\in S^{\perp}$ and $u=\sum_i\lambda_i s_i$ is a finite linear combination
  with $s_i\in S$, then linearity in the second argument gives
  $\eta(v,u)=\sum_i\lambda_i\eta(v,s_i)=0$, so $v\in(\operatorname{span}S)^{\perp}$.

In particular, for every $u\in V$ one has $u\in u^{\perp}$ exactly when
$\eta(u,u)=0$, that is, exactly when $u$ is null or $u=0$
([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]).

**A nonzero vector can be orthogonal to itself.** Take a basis
$e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$ of $V$ in which the matrix of $\eta$ is diagonal with
diagonal entries $-1,1,1,1$; such a basis exists by clause 2 of the definition
of a Lorentz form. Then $v:=e_0+e_1$ is nonzero while
$\eta(v,v)=\eta(e_0,e_0)+2\eta(e_0,e_1)+\eta(e_1,e_1)=-1+0+1=0$, so
$v\in v^{\perp}$ with $v\neq 0$. This is exactly what fails for a
positive-definite inner product and is why orthogonal complements in a Lorentz
vector space need not be positive definite.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]), with associated quadratic form
$q(v)=\eta(v,v)$. A vector $v\in V$ is

- **timelike** when $q(v)<0$;
- **null**, or **lightlike**, when $v\neq 0$ and $q(v)=0$;
- **spacelike** when $q(v)>0$;
- **causal** when it is timelike or null.

The zero vector $0\in V$ satisfies $q(0)=0$ and is consequently **none** of
timelike, null or spacelike: the null case explicitly excludes it, and the
timelike and spacelike cases exclude it by $q(0)=0$ together with the strict
inequalities. The **causal character** of a nonzero vector $v$ is the sign of
the real number $q(v)$, and the three names are attached to the three signs as
above. When no confusion arises, the pairing $\eta$ itself is written
$\langle v,w\rangle:=\eta(v,w)$.

**Each nonzero vector has exactly one causal character.** For a nonzero
$v\in V$ the real number $q(v)$ satisfies exactly one of $q(v)<0$, $q(v)=0$,
$q(v)>0$ by trichotomy of the order on $\mathbb R$, so $v$ is timelike, null or
spacelike, and no two of the three alternatives can hold at once. The causal
vectors are therefore exactly the nonzero vectors that are timelike or null,
and the zero vector is causal in no sense introduced here.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]), with causal terminology as in
[[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]], and let

$$T:=\{v\in V:\eta(v,v)<0\}$$

be its **timelike set**. By [[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]] the
set $T$ has exactly two connected components, and each of them is nonempty,
open, convex and path-connected. A **time orientation** of $(V,\eta)$ is a
choice of one of these two components. Fixing such a choice, write $C^+$ for the
chosen component and

$$C^-:=T\setminus C^+$$

for the other component; thus $T=C^+\sqcup C^-$ is a disjoint union and
$C^+$, $C^-$ are exactly the two components supplied by the lemma. Relative to
this choice a vector $v\in V$ is

- **future timelike** when $v\in C^+$;
- **past timelike** when $v\in C^-$;
- **future null** when $v\neq 0$, $\eta(v,v)=0$ and $v\in\operatorname{cl}(C^+)$;
- **past null** when $v\neq 0$, $\eta(v,v)=0$ and $v\in\operatorname{cl}(C^-)$;
- **future causal** when it is future timelike or future null;
- **past causal** when it is past timelike or past null.

The sets $\operatorname{cl}(C^+)$ and $\operatorname{cl}(C^-)$ are the
**future closed cone** and the **past closed cone** of the time-oriented space
$(V,\eta,C^+)$. By [[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]] each of them
is a convex cone, their intersection is $\{0\}$, and a vector is causal exactly
when it is future causal or past causal, in which case exactly one of these two
alternatives holds: no nonzero vector is both future causal and past causal.
The timelike vectors are exactly the points of $T=C^+\cup C^-$, and
$0\notin T$ because $\eta(0,0)=0$; since a null vector is nonzero with
$\eta(v,v)=0$, no vector is both timelike and null, so the classes above are
mutually exclusive where the definitions say they are: no vector is both future
and past causal, and no timelike vector is null.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$ and let
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an $\eta$-orthonormal ordered basis. Write
$v=v^0e_0+v^1e_1+v^2e_2+v^3e_3$ for the coordinates of $v$
([[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]) and

$$\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert:=\sqrt{(v^1)^2+(v^2)^2+(v^3)^2}.$$

Then $\eta(v,v)=-(v^0)^2+\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert^2$, and the timelike set
$T:=\{v\in V:\eta(v,v)<0\}$ satisfies

$$T=T_+\cup T_-,\qquad T_+:=\{v:v^0>\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\},\qquad T_-:=\{v:v^0<-\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\}.$$

The sets $T_+$ and $T_-$ are nonempty, disjoint, open in $V$ (for the metric
topology of the distance $d(u,w):=\lVert c(u)-c(w)\rVert_2$ induced by the
coordinates $c(v):=(v^0,v^1,v^2,v^3)$), convex and path-connected, and they are
exactly the two connected components of $T$. In every $\eta$-orthonormal
ordered basis the two displayed coordinate sets coincide with the two
components of $T$ in some order, and they may be interchanged relative to a
previously fixed naming of the components. Moreover

$$\operatorname{cl}(T_+)=\{v:v^0\ge\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\},\qquad \operatorname{cl}(T_-)=\{v:v^0\le-\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\},\qquad \operatorname{cl}(T_+)\cap\operatorname{cl}(T_-)=\{0\}.$$

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

On $u^{\perp}$, substituting $v^1=2v^0$ into the quadratic form gives $\eta(v,v)=-(v^0)^2+4(v^0)^2+(v^2)^2+(v^3)^2=3(v^0)^2+(v^2)^2+(v^3)^2$, a sum of nonnegative terms; it vanishes exactly when $v^0=v^2=v^3=0$, and then also $v^1=2v^0=0$, so $v=0$. Thus the orthogonal complement of this timelike displacement is genuinely positive definite, in contrast with the null case.

$\Phi_p(v)$ is a derivation at $p$: for smooth germs $[f],[g]$, the coordinate representatives satisfy $((fg)\circ x^{-1})=(f\circ x^{-1})(g\circ x^{-1})$, so the one-variable product rule [L5a] applied to the differentiable functions $t\mapsto F(y+te_a)$ and $t\mapsto G(y+te_a)$ gives the product rule for the partial derivatives: $\partial_a((fg)\circ x^{-1})(x(p))=f(p)\partial_a(g\circ x^{-1})(x(p))+g(p)\partial_a(f\circ x^{-1})(x(p))$, since $f(x^{-1}(x(p)))=f(p)$ and likewise for $g$; substituting into step 2.1 gives $\Phi_p(v)([f][g])=f(p)\Phi_p(v)([g])+g(p)\Phi_p(v)([f])$, so $\Phi_p(v)\in T_pA$ by [L1].

Applying $\Phi_p(v)$ to the germ of the coordinate function $x^a$ gives, by step 2.1, $\Phi_p(v)([x^a])=\sum_bu^b\partial_b(x^a\circ x^{-1})(x(p))=\sum_bu^b\delta^a_b=u^a$; hence $u=0$, and since $E^{-1}$ is injective by [L6], $v=0$.

$\Phi_p$ carries the basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $V$ to the coordinate derivations: for $v=e_a$ one has $u=E^{-1}(e_a)=(\delta^a_b)_b$ by [L6], so step 2.1 gives $\Phi_p(e_a)([f])=\partial_aF(x(p))=\partial_a|_p([f])$ for every smooth germ, that is, $\Phi_p(e_a)=\partial_a|_p$. By [L5] the derivations $\partial_a|_p$ form a basis of $T_pA$, so the linear map $\Phi_p$ carries a basis of $V$ to a basis of $T_pA$; hence $\Phi_p$ is surjective (its image contains a basis) and injective by step 3.3, so it is a linear isomorphism $V\to T_pA$.

Finally, let $v=\sum_av^ae_a$; then $u=E^{-1}(v)=(v^0,v^1,v^2,v^3)$, so step 2.1 gives $\Phi_p(v)([f])=\sum_av^a\partial_aF(x(p))$, that is, $\Phi_p(v)=\sum_av^a\partial_a|_p$.
